A $10 billion fund opened a stake in MercadoLibre and added to Snowflake and Ciena in the third quarter, its latest 13F shows.

All three stocks are down since Sept. 30: MercadoLibre by 22% and Ciena by 33%.

Analysts' average price targets are 59% to 118% above today's prices.

Snowflake has the strongest case of the three, because analysts keep raising its estimates and it trades below its usual multiple.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ), Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE) and Ciena (CIEN:NYSE) were the biggest new and added positions at SCGE Management in the third quarter. That's according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13. All three cost less today.

The firm manages $10.4 billion in all, according to its latest Form ADV. Its 13F showed $4.83 billion of US stocks across 21 positions.

MercadoLibre is cheap, and estimates are still falling

At Sept. 30, the fund held 70,000 MercadoLibre shares worth $121 million. It was a new position and made up 2.5% of its 13F stocks. The stock is down 22% from its Sept. 30 price and 42% below its 52-week high.

The problem is margins. Third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but the GAAP operating margin fell to 6.3% from 9.8%. The company spent more on free shipping, fulfillment space and marketing in Brazil. Management wouldn't give a margin target on the call, and analysts have cut their 2026 EPS estimate by more than 40% since September 2025.

That puts the stock at about 31x forward earnings. Its average since 2023 is 48x, and it's now below even its March low of 33x. Analysts have been cutting their price targets all year:

Key Takeaways

Bank of America cut its MercadoLibre price target to $2,000 from $2,400 on Nov. 19 and kept its Buy rating, 48% above the Nov. 20 close.

MercadoLibre is giving up margin to stay ahead of rivals, including Sea Limited's Shopee in Brazil and Nu Holdings in credit.

On 2028 earnings estimates, $2,000 is 27x, below any forward multiple the stock has traded at in five years.

The valuation looks fair, but estimates keep falling, so $2,000 will likely take more than 12 months to reach.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) stock has lost 29% in a year, closing at $1,355.00 on Nov. 20. On Nov. 19, Bank of America cut its price target to $2,000 from $2,400 and kept its Buy rating, 48% above that close. The bank also lowered its 2026 to 2028 EPS estimates, saying the company is putting off monetization to reinvest in its lead.

MercadoLibre is spending heavily against two well-funded rivals: Sea Limited (SE:NYSE)'s Shopee in Brazil, and Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE) in credit.

A margin MercadoLibre chose to give up

Sea can afford the fight. Shopee's adjusted EBITDA rose 44.7% to $269.2 million in the third quarter, its most profitable quarter ever. Sea CEO Forrest Li said Brazil remained Shopee's fastest-growing market, and its new instant delivery service there already delivers in under four hours from more than 7,000 partner stores.

MercadoLibre's Nov. 4 report showed the cost of keeping up. Revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but GAAP operating income fell 6.6% to $676 million. That's a 6.3% margin, against 9.8% a year earlier. Management tied the drop to more free shipping, nearly 20% more fulfillment space added from the prior quarter ahead of peak season, and heavier affiliate marketing in Brazil.

Bank of America is betting on the card

Analyst Robert Ford Aguilar has made Mercado Pago's credit card a big part of his case. In a June note, he forecast a $443 million EBIT loss on the card in 2026, breakeven in 2028 and $1.5 billion of EBIT by 2030. He put MercadoLibre's share of Brazil's card balances at 3.4% in March. Nu's credit portfolio rose 33% in a year, FX-neutral, while MercadoLibre's rose 62%, to almost $18 billion.

title: Chewy vs. MercadoLibre: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Chewy vs. MercadoLibre: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 10:20 AM MST 7 min read
CHWY
MELI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Does the stability of the pet category outweigh the high growth of Latin American e-commerce? Choosing between Chewy Inc. (NYSE:CHWY) and MercadoLibre Inc. (NASDAQ:MELI) requires balancing recurring revenue against regional market dominance.

Chewy focuses on the North American pet market through specialized fulfillment and a high-margin subscription model. MercadoLibre operates a massive integrated commerce and fintech ecosystem across 18 countries in Latin America. Investors often compare them to see if a niche leader or a geographic titan offers better long-term potential.

The case for Chewy

Chewy operates as a leading online retailer for pet owners, providing everything from food and toys to prescription medications. The company partners with approximately 4,000 brands and has developed its own private labels such as Frisco and American Journey. A significant portion of its business comes from the PracticeHub platform, which is currently used by roughly 50% of all veterinary clinics in the United States. This specialized focus among retail stocks allows the company to build deep loyalty through subscription-like programs.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached about $13.1 billion. This represented growth of roughly 5.9% compared to the prior twelve-month period. Net income for the period was about $273.7 million, as the company continues to focus on improving profitability through its high-margin Autoship subscription service and pharmacy sales.

As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, meaning total debt is equal to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, is roughly 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, free cash flow was around $562.4 million. Note that for the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, stock-based compensation represented roughly 43.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since stock-based compensation is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for MercadoLibre

MercadoLibre provides an integrated commerce and financial services ecosystem across 18 different countries in Latin America. Its Marketplace platform facilitates both direct sales and third-party transactions, supported by an extensive logistics network known as Mercado Envios. The company also operates Mercado Pago, a fintech powerhouse that handles online payments, credit, and asset management for millions of users. By combining these services, the company captures growth from both the rise of digital shopping and the increasing adoption of digital financial tools in emerging markets.

Investing.com — Brazil's presidential election has been expensive for anyone holding the country's stocks. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's fourth-term victory on October 26 sent the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (NYSEARCA:EWZ) crashing nearly 19% and dragged Nu Holdings (NYSE:NU) down with it, as investors weighed public debt above 82% of GDP. MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI)—Latin America's dominant e-commerce and fintech platform—has not escaped either, crashing 27.9% over the past month to $1,355.49, including a 9.1% slide in the past week alone.

MercadoLibre's sales are still booming, but the company is paying for that growth with its own margins. Analysts forecast 44.3% revenue growth, yet consensus calls for EPS to shrink 6.9% as free-shipping subsidies, fulfillment center buildouts, and a fast-growing credit card book squeeze operating margins, leaving the stock at 36.4 times trailing earnings. InvestingPro's valuation models flag the shares as "Undervalued" at $1,668.90, a 23.1% implied upside. That leaves dip-buyers betting on a margin recovery management has not yet put a date on.

The Ecosystem That Turns Shoppers Into Borrowers

MercadoLibre makes its money by tying a marketplace, a payments network, a logistics arm, a lending book, and an ad business into one ecosystem—and every service it adds makes the others harder to leave. Users active in both commerce and fintech generate 70% more GMV and 90% more payment volume than single-platform users, and that cohort grew 37% year-over-year in the second quarter.

Third-quarter results confirmed that demand is not the problem. Revenue climbed 45% year-over-year to $10.75 billion, topping the $10.69 billion estimate, as GMV rose 38% to $23 billion and payment volume surged 53% to $109 billion. The credit book expanded 62% to nearly $18 billion, with non-performing loans near historical lows across products and regions.

The cash is going straight back into the buildout. Operating cash flow reached $13.9 billion over the trailing twelve months, but the second quarter showed how much the investment cycle absorbs—adjusted free cash flow was just $214 million after $441 million in capex and $2.1 billion invested in credit book growth.

Fair Value Says Cheap, The Margins Say Wait

Wall Street remains bullish, but it is trimming its numbers. The consensus is Strong Buy, with 9 Buys and 3 Holds and a median price target of about $2,210. After the third quarter, Scotiabank cut its target to $2,300 from $2,800, Cantor Fitzgerald to $2,000 from $2,200, and Raymond James to $2,000 from $2,100, while UBS holds at $1,600 and JPMorgan at $1,850. Every one of those targets sits above the current share price, yet 4 of the last 5 EPS revisions over the past 90 days have moved lower.

InvestingPro's Fair Value models make the bull case, placing intrinsic value at $1,668.90 per share—23.1% above the share price but well below the Street's median target.

The flaws sit in the margin line. Third-quarter EPS of $8.83 missed the $9.34 consensus by 5.5%, and operating margin compressed to 6.3% from 12.2% a year earlier and 7.0% in the prior quarter. Fulfillment square footage grew almost 20% quarter-over-quarter, lower free-shipping thresholds in Brazil raised per-shipment costs, and sales and marketing climbed to 11.6% of revenue from 11.2%.

The regional and credit risks stack on top. Mexico's FX-neutral GMV grew only 21% amid tax reform and weak consumption, and the credit card book's net interest margin after losses turned negative at -2.5% in the second quarter as MercadoLibre issued 2.6 million cards, up from 1.6 million a year earlier. Rapid lending growth across 18 countries leaves earnings exposed to any turn in the credit cycle.

Growth Is Not the Question, Margins Are

MercadoLibre's ecosystem keeps drawing in more shoppers, sellers, and borrowers every quarter. Investors who buy now are funding the logistics and credit buildout alongside management, and the share price is likely to stay under pressure until the spending starts showing up in earnings.

A fund that manages $10.4 billion made its biggest Q3 moves in three growth stocks that have all fallen hard since: MercadoLibre, Snowflake and Ciena.

SCGE Management's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13, shows a new position in MercadoLibre and bigger stakes in the other two.

They were the largest of the four positions it opened or added to. In all, the 13F lists $4.83 billion of US stocks across 21 positions.

A 13F doesn't show what the fund paid, but all three stocks are cheaper now than they were on Sept. 30.

MercadoLibre's margin keeps sliding

MercadoLibre was the only brand-new position of the three. The fund held 70,000 shares worth $121 million at Sept. 30, which was 2.5% of SCGE's 13F holdings and its ninth-biggest holding. The stock is down 22% since then and sits 42% below its 52-week high.

Sales aren't the issue. Q3 revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion. But the GAAP operating margin fell to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier, and management blamed more free shipping, more fulfillment space, and extra marketing in Brazil.

Snowflake's growth is speeding up

While MercadoLibre's estimates are falling, Snowflake's are climbing. SCGE added 65% to its stake and ended the quarter with 331,900 shares worth $113 million. That was 2.3% of its 13F holdings and its 10th-biggest holding. The stock is down 23% since Sept. 30.

Product revenue grew 37% to $1.49 billion in the quarter ended July 31, the third straight quarter of faster growth. Management credits AI products with about half of that pickup.

It raised its fiscal 2027 product revenue outlook to $6.07 billion, from $5.66 billion in February. Analysts' normalized EPS estimate for fiscal 2027 has risen to $2.23 from $1.94 over the past 90 days, and their average target has climbed with it:

Snowflake (SNOW): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

It's $433 now, near its high for the year and up from $271 a year ago. That's 61% above the stock.

The price is the catch. At about 106x forward earnings, Snowflake trades below its 124x average of the past year, but investors paying that are counting on the AI growth to keep coming.

AI is also thinning the margin. Non-GAAP product gross margin fell to 74% from 76% a year earlier, and management cut its full-year outlook to 74% from 75%.

Ciena's business held up better than its stock

Ciena got SCGE's biggest increase of the three: 85% more shares, for 164,300 shares worth $58 million at Sept. 30. That's 1.2% of its 13F holdings and its 15th-biggest holding. The stock has fallen the most since, down 29%, and it sits 59% below its 52-week high.

There's little in Ciena's own numbers to explain that. In fiscal Q3 ended Aug. 1, revenue rose 37% to $1.7 billion and adjusted EPS rose to $2.11 from $0.67.

Ciena also raised its fiscal 2026 revenue outlook to $6.42 billion, plus or minus $50 million, from $6.3 billion.

Instead, the stock fell with the rest of AI hardware after Democrats swept the midterms, on fears that a Democratic Congress could slow data-center construction.

UBS estimated that nearly a third of the new US capacity due in 2028 could be delayed if construction pauses spread.

Analysts haven't followed the stock down:

Their average target is $512. That's more than triple the $155 of last December, not far off June's peak of $566, and 95% above the stock.

Ciena is the one I'd follow

If I could only buy one of these right now, it'd be Ciena.

Its results and its outlook both point up; it trades at about 25x forward earnings, and the stock fell on a worry about data-center construction that its own numbers don't show yet.

If those projects do slow, Ciena's orders will feel it. So its report in December needs fiscal Q4 revenue near the $1.75 billion it guided.

Snowflake comes second for me. The estimates are rising, but at that price, its early-December report has to show product revenue at or above its $1.588-$1.593 billion guide for the quarter.

MercadoLibre is the cheapest against its own history. At about 31x forward earnings, it trades below the 48x it averaged at quarter-ends since 2023, and below its March low of 33x.

But analysts have cut their 2026 EPS estimate 42% since September 2025. On the Q3 call, CFO Martin de los Santos wouldn't give a margin target: "The approach is to manage for the long term." Until the operating margin stops falling, I'd wait.

Of course, SCGE's next 13F, due in mid-February, will show whether it added to any of the three.

The two payment networks have gone the other way. The fund held 84,800 Mastercard shares on Sept. 30, 20% more than at June 30. They were worth $47 million, or 2.0% of its 13F stocks, and the stock has gained 14% since.

Mastercard's services revenue grew 19% in the third quarter, and its total revenue grew 14%. More than a dozen firms raised their targets after the report, J.P. Morgan to $755 from $720 among them. The average target has climbed from $657 a year ago to $721, its high for the year.

Visa, at about 27x, sits right at its 28x average. The $15.02 of fiscal 2027 EPS analysts expect is at the top of Visa's guided range and only 4% above the $14.47 they expected a year ago, so there's little room for a miss.

Mastercard is the add to follow

The risk with Mastercard is what it costs to win business. Rebates and incentives rose 18% in the third quarter, and Mastercard expects them to take a larger share of its fees in the fourth.

Even so, if I could only follow one of these adds, it'd be Mastercard. Its estimates and targets are rising, and it still trades below its usual multiple. MercadoLibre has far more upside on paper, and a margin recovery would make it the better buy, but I'd want to see its estimates stop falling first.

The fund's next 13F is due in mid-February and will show whether it kept adding to MercadoLibre as the stock fell. Before that, MercadoLibre's fourth-quarter report early next year is the test. Its CFO said part of the new fulfillment costs should "come back in Q4." An operating margin back toward the 10.1% of a year earlier would make 2027's estimates look reachable again.

Can MercadoLibre's GMV Growth Fuel Long-Term Earnings Gains?
Sumit Singh

SE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI continues to build momentum in Latin America's e-commerce market, supported by higher purchase frequency, expanding customer engagement and improving logistics efficiency. In third-quarter 2026, gross merchandise volume (GMV) reached $22.8 billion, increasing 38% year over year on a reported basis and 33% on an FX-neutral basis, while items sold rose 36% to 867 million. Unique active buyers increased approximately 22.3% to 93.9 million, highlighting sustained marketplace adoption and deeper customer engagement.

Brazil remains a major growth driver, with FX-neutral GMV advancing 36% and items sold rising 45%. The company's lower free-shipping threshold continues to encourage more frequent purchases, with items per buyer increasing 16% year over year. Management also reported stronger retention among customer cohorts acquired after the threshold reduction. However, smaller baskets and more free shipments have reduced shipping revenue per shipment. As a result, net shipping margin as a percentage of GMV has declined approximately 200 basis points since first-quarter 2025.

Meanwhile, Brazil's cost per shipment fell 5% year over year in local currency and 14% compared with first-quarter 2025, reflecting improving logistics efficiency. In September, free and slow shipments in the R$19-R$79 price range became variable contribution-positive for the first time. MercadoLibre is also expanding its logistics capabilities, having opened 13 Metro fulfillment centers over the past 12 months and more than doubled the number of sorters and robots across its network. Management expects higher shipment density, automation and better network utilization to drive further cost improvements.

Still, stronger GMV growth has yet to translate fully into operating profitability. Third-quarter operating income declined 6% year over year to $676 million, while the operating margin reached 6.3%, down 40 basis points sequentially. Net shipping costs created a 60-basis-point margin headwind, reflecting increased free shipping, higher energy expenses and additional fulfillment capacity. Increased affiliate marketing investments in Brazil also pressured margins. Nevertheless, net income rose 6% to $448 million, supported by a lower tax rate and reduced foreign-exchange losses.

Management expects improving logistics productivity and greater operating scale to gradually reduce shipping costs relative to business volumes. MercadoLibre's ability to sustain purchase frequency while lowering fulfillment costs remains central to translating marketplace growth into stronger long-term earnings.

Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre (MELI) stock fell approximately 20% from October 5 to November 10, closing at $1,490.24 after reaching a new 52-week low on November 5.

MercadoLibre's third-quarter revenue and financial income rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but operating margin declined to 6.3% as shipping, fulfillment, and marketing investments pressured profitability.

Sea Limited (SE) reported 41.3% revenue growth at Shopee in the third quarter, while Nu Holdings (NU) provides another perspective on Brazilian consumer credit conditions.

MercadoLibre appears potentially undervalued following the selloff, although stronger margins and continued market share gains will be important to a sustained recovery.

What Happened?

MercadoLibre (MELI) stock declined approximately 20% from its October 5 closing price of $1,860.61 to $1,490.24 on November 10, after hitting a new 52-week low on November 5.

The decline reflects two concerns: political uncertainty in Brazil and weaker-than-expected profitability despite strong revenue growth.

Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff delivered another term for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who defeated Flávio Bolsonaro after trailing him in the first round.

MercadoLibre shares fell approximately 8% on October 26 as investors reassessed Brazil's economic outlook, currency risks, and consumer spending conditions.

Brazil generated approximately $15.2 billion of MercadoLibre's $28.9 billion in 2025 revenue, making it the company's largest market.

However, the company's third-quarter earnings report created a more immediate concern.

According to MercadoLibre's third-quarter financial results, revenue and financial income increased 45% year over year to $10.75 billion, but reported earnings of $8.83 per share fell short of the $9.27 consensus estimate cited in the initial research brief.

Operating margin declined to 6.3% from approximately 9.8% a year earlier, reflecting higher shipping expenses, expanded fulfillment capacity, and increased marketing spending in Brazil.

In its third-quarter shareholder letter, management described the pressure on shipping margins as "the price of the habit we set out to build."

The strategy is producing results. Items sold in Brazil increased more than 40% year over year for the fifth consecutive quarter, while MercadoLibre gained market share across its three largest markets.

Its lower free-shipping threshold also encouraged smaller purchases, initially putting pressure on shipping economics.

By September, Brazilian orders valued between R$19 and R$79 that qualified for free or slower delivery became variable contribution-positive for the first time, suggesting higher order volumes are beginning to improve shipping economics.
